title: Vongole in Bianco
subtitle: Clams in white wine, garlic, and parsley
excerpt: Vongole in bianco is clams cooked open in white wine with garlic, olive oil, and parsley, served without pasta as a standalone starter. The clams open in under 5 minutes and produce a concentrated, briny broth that is part of the dish. The key is to serve them immediately, in their shells, with bread.
sourceNotes: Clams prepared in white wine (vongole in bianco) is one of the classic preparations of the Italian coast, common from Liguria to Campania. It is the base for spaghetti alle vongole but is equally served as an antipasto in its own right. The Vongola verace (true clam, Venus verrucosa) is the prized species in Campania; palourdes or Manila clams are the standard substitution elsewhere.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Soak the clams in salted water for 30 minutes before cooking to purge sand. Cook and serve immediately.

glossaryTerms.definition: Soaking live clams in cold, lightly salted water for 30 minutes so they filter out sand from their shells before cooking.

content.text: Vongole in bianco is clams cooked open in white wine, garlic, and olive oil. It is the dish that becomes spaghetti alle vongole when pasta is added, but it stands on its own as a starter: the clams are served in their shells in the cooking liquid, with bread to soak up the broth. to remove any sand is the only advance work needed.

items.prepNote: soaked in cold salted water for 30 minutes, drained and rinsed

content.text: Soak the clams in cold water with a tablespoon of salt for 30 minutes. Drain, rinse, and discard any that are cracked or do not close when tapped.
Heat the olive oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the garlic and chilli if using. Cook for 2 minutes until the garlic is pale gold.
Increase the heat to high. Add the white wine and let it bubble for 30 seconds.
Add the clams and put the lid on. Cook for 3 to 5 minutes, shaking the pan occasionally, until all the clams have opened. Discard any that remain closed.
Scatter the parsley over the top and add a crack of black pepper. Serve immediately in deep bowls with the broth, and good bread to mop it up.

Clams in white wine is common from Liguria down to Campania and around Sicily. The Neapolitan version, vongole verace, uses a small local clam that is sweeter and less briny than the palourdes widely available in northern Europe. Both are excellent prepared this way. The purging soak is essential: clams that have not been purged release sand into the broth and make the dish gritty.
